digest.intro: War reshapes information space; biology rewrites what bodies can do.

items.title: Europe Blacks Out Satellite Imagery of the Strait of Hormuz at US Request
items.blurb: The EU has imposed a 24-hour delay on all Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery covering the Gulf of Oman — a break from Copernicus's foundational open-data principle, triggered by a US request made May 26 during a ceasefire that has since collapsed. Iran, lacking access to Western commercial imagery, has turned to Chinese satellites to track US military bases. The information blackout is now a theater of war as real as the strikes.

items.title: Iran Rejects US Ceasefire Proposal as Escalation Signals Mount
items.blurb: Stratfor's July 25 weekly assessment flags Iran's rejection of the latest US ceasefire proposal and notes the US military resumed broader strikes on July 8 after a shaky pause. Two parallel tracks dominate this week: the Iran escalation and Zelensky in Washington, with the fall of Kostiantynivka potentially shifting Ukraine's eastern front simultaneously. Both threads are moving faster than diplomatic bandwidth can absorb.

items.title: First-in-Human Trial: Immune-Engineered Insulin Cells Without Immunosuppression
items.blurb: Presented at ISSCR 2026, Sonja Schrepfer's Cedars-Sinai team is asking in actual humans whether hypoimmune-engineered allogeneic insulin-producing cells can survive without the chronic immunosuppression that has always been the deal-breaker for islet transplantation. The engineering trick is making the cells effectively invisible to the immune system — no suppression, no rejection cascade. Still early, but this is the question that has blocked a T1D functional cure for decades, now being tested in people.

items.title: Supercooled Pig Kidneys Survived Days at −4°C and Were Successfully Reimplanted
items.blurb: The organ preservation field is having a genuinely productive moment: pig kidneys — similar in size to human kidneys — were supercooled to −4°C without forming ice, stored for days, and then reimplanted successfully. The fundamental problem is that ice crystals destroy cells, and the challenge of scaling cryopreservation from eggs and embryos (routine) to whole organs (still unsolved) is essentially a materials and perfusion engineering problem. The dream of organ banks — stored, matchable, transportable — is getting less dreamlike.

items.title: AlphaFold Helped Redesign Gene-Editing Proteins to Eliminate Off-Target Cuts
items.blurb: Off-target editing — CRISPR cutting the wrong sequence — is low-probability per cell but becomes statistically inevitable when you're editing millions of cells in a therapy. Researchers modified AlphaFold to identify the specific structural regions of Cas proteins responsible for that promiscuity, then redesigned those regions to eliminate it. Published in Nature, this is AI-as-protein-engineer working on a real therapeutic bottleneck, not a benchmark.

items.title: The Peptide Deregulation Decision Has No Human Safety Data Behind It
items.blurb: An FDA advisory panel — assembled under RFK Jr., who personally uses several of the peptides in question — voted to lift manufacturing restrictions on four peptides despite no adequate human safety or efficacy trials. The mechanism here is institutional: change the committee composition, change the vote, change the policy, skip the science. Worth understanding as context for the entire current peptide access moment — this is the regulatory structure behind it.

items.title: CMU Snake Robots Had Their First Real Humanitarian Deployment in Venezuela
items.blurb: After two earthquakes killed 5,000+ people in Venezuela on June 24, Howie Choset's Biorobotics Lab sent their 4-foot modular snake robots into the rubble — 20 years of iteration meeting its first live humanitarian test. The robots are human-directed via game controller but use autonomous gait algorithms to coordinate body segments through the specific geometry of collapsed concrete. What struck the CMU nurse-responder on the ground wasn't skepticism from rescue teams: it was the opposite — first responders were hungry for tools that solve real problems without adding complexity.

items.title: The Most Advanced Robotic Servicing Satellite — That We Know About
items.blurb: Northrop Grumman's Mission Robotic Vehicle launched this week on a Falcon 9 — two flexible robotic arms, a decade-long mission in geosynchronous orbit, and three companion propulsion pods that function as standalone spacecraft for satellite life-extension. The 'that we know about' qualifier is doing real work: China launched a satellite with a robotic arm into GEO in 2016, and its 2021 Shijian-21 grabbed a defunct navigation satellite and moved it to a graveyard orbit. Dexterous manipulation in the hardest possible environment, with obvious dual-use implications nobody is quite saying aloud.

items.title: Psychedelics Probably Didn't Evolve for Humans — or Even for Consciousness
items.blurb: A new PNAS study argues that psilocybin, mescaline, DMT, and related compounds evolved as ecological tools — predator deterrents, symbiosis managers — and that human hallucination is simply a side effect of shared serotonin receptor chemistry with snails, sea urchins, and sponges. The entire edifice of co-evolution mythology (psychedelic plants 'meant' for human spiritual use) deflates into a much stranger story: the molecules are ancient, promiscuous, and indifferent to our visions. The therapeutic value survives this explanation intact — it just stops being cosmic.

facts.fact: Iran has been sourcing satellite imagery of US military bases from China after being cut off from Western commercial imagery providers during the ongoing conflict.
CMU's snake robots are modular — individual body segments can be swapped in the field — and a single operator controls the whole system with a standard video game controller.

Tiny amounts of DMT are naturally produced in human brains, but a new PNAS study argues this is an evolutionary accident of shared receptor chemistry rather than evidence of a special visionary function.

Pig kidneys supercooled to −4°C survived for days without ice crystal formation and were successfully reimplanted — a barrier that has blocked whole-organ preservation for transplantation for decades.

China's Shijian-21 spacecraft grappled a defunct Chinese navigation satellite in orbit and moved it to a higher disposal orbit before returning — the same dexterous capability the new Northrop Grumman servicing satellite is designed to offer commercially.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film built entirely from the gap between image and memory — Marker uses found footage, letters, and a narrator to construct a meditation on how cultures encode time, ritual, and identity. It moves like a notebook from someone who went unreasonably deep on the invisible systems underneath ordinary life; exactly the kind of rabbit-hole essay Willem craves.

art_picks.title: The Unilever Series: Olafur Eliasson — The Weather Project
art_picks.creator: Olafur Eliasson
art_picks.why: A sun made of mono-frequency lamps and a mirrored ceiling that turned Tate Modern's Turbine Hall into a collective ritual — strangers lying on the floor staring at themselves and a fake sun. The piece is about how a shared physical environment manufactures collective experience; art functioning as community infrastructure, which is exactly the edge Willem works near.

art_picks.title: Vespertine
art_picks.creator: Björk
art_picks.why: A completely self-consistent micro-world built from music boxes, harps, choir, and beats so intimate they sound biological — Björk went unreasonably deep on one emotional register (interiority, domestic tenderness) and built a whole sonic system around it. The physical/digital boundary doesn't exist here; everything sounds both handmade and machine-processed at once.

events.name: Whitney Biennial 2026
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, Manhattan
events.why: Still on through August 23 and currently coinciding with both Greater New York and the upcoming New Museum Triennial — a rare triple convergence that won't happen again for years; worth going now while the city's curatorial conversation is at full volume.

events.name: Greater New York 2026
events.venue: MoMA PS1, Long Island City, Queens
events.why: The quinquennial snapshot of what artists actually living in NYC are making right now — 53 artists, 150+ works spanning painting to animation to scenography, organized around surveillance, economic precarity, and shifting technology, all while free to attend; a rare chance to see the city's creative nervous system mid-fire.

events.name: Gabriel Orozco: Public Nature
events.venue: JCDecaux Bus Shelters across New York City
events.why: Orozco's first major public art show in NYC is also his first commissioned photographic series — 10 new site-specific images about urban fabric appearing in bus shelters across the city, turning the most anonymous infrastructure of daily life into a gallery; art distributed through the city's invisible logistics system is precisely Willem's territory.

events.name: Man Man + Death Valley Girls
events.why: Man Man are maximalist, theatrical, and impossible to categorize — they treat performance as ritual and noise as craft; tonight's pairing with Death Valley Girls is a genuine double bill of bands who treat weirdness as a system, not a pose.

events.name: Andrew Bird + Wordless Music Orchestra — 20th Anniversary of The Mysterious Production of Eggs
events.why: Bird performing the full album live for the first time ever, with a full orchestra — a record built on loops, multi-tracked violin, and elaborate systems that was ahead of its time; hearing it realized at orchestral scale in a park at night is the kind of thing you don't get twice, and it's free.
